Guided trip

Asteroids, and the ones that come close

The belt, the rocks that pass us, and how we moved one. Then back to Earth.

Open the trip: Asteroids, and the ones that come close

The asteroid belt

Between the paths of Mars and Jupiter there are more than a million rocks, left over from the making of the planets about four and a half billion years ago. It is mostly empty space: all of them together weigh less than our Moon. The map draws the few it carries, each where it is today.

Ceres, the largest

Ceres is about nine hundred and fifty kilometres across and holds a quarter of the belt's whole mass. It is round, so it counts as a dwarf planet. A spacecraft called Dawn reached it in 2015, the first visit to a dwarf planet, and found large deposits of salt in its crust.

The ones that come close

Some asteroids have paths that bring them near the Earth's. More than forty thousand have been found, ten thousand of them in the last three years. Telescopes find them, and each one's path is worked out for a hundred years ahead. The line below names the next one to pass.

The asteroid we moved

Didymos has a small moon. In 2022 a spacecraft called DART was flown straight into that moon at more than six kilometres a second, on purpose. Its orbit became thirty-two minutes shorter. It was the first time people changed the motion of anything in the sky.

Hera, going to check

This is Hera, a European spacecraft sent to the same pair of asteroids, due there in November 2026. It will survey the little moon after the crash and measure its mass, to turn that one experiment into a method that can be repeated if a dangerous rock is ever found.

Bennu, and a handful brought home

Bennu is about half a kilometre wide. A spacecraft touched it, collected a hundred and twenty grams, and dropped them in the Utah desert in 2023: the largest asteroid sample ever brought home. In that dust were sugars and other molecules that, on Earth, are key to life.

Apophis passes the Earth

One pass is already in the calendar. This rock, Apophis, is about three hundred and forty metres across, and this is the evening it comes closest: about thirty-two thousand kilometres above the ground, inside the ring of satellites that carry television. It will miss. The path drawn here is the one predicted at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory.

Are we safe?

For the large ones, yes. The vast majority of the asteroids bigger than a kilometre have been found, and none of the forty thousand known is a threat in the next hundred years. But only about a third of the middle-sized ones have been found. The search goes on.

Everything is drawn where it really is, from the planets’ own orbits (astronomy-engine).
